kalevalarunosong.basis: Archive side: SKVR holds over 89,000 Kalevala-metre texts but these are texts, not recordings; SKS sound archives (wax cylinders from 1905, tapes) hold more field recordings, few issued commercially (Ondine's Kalevala Heritage spans 1905-1967). Revival side: a handful of specialist singers (Korhonen, Hoffrén, Kurki-Suonio, Turkka, Langeland, Käppi) each with a few runo-based albums. Estimate of issued, listenable tracks is a rough count, not a catalogue total.

ngoma.basis: Mostly archive holdings: ILAM/SAMAP list hundreds of Hugh Tracey 1950s Tanganyika and Kenya dance-song items tagged drum or ngoma dance (the Sukuma listing alone runs to a dozen pages, Gogo four), plus a handful of commercial field-recording albums (SWP, Caprice, Acoustic Music, Honest Jon's, Real World). Commercial releases number only in the tens; the core reflects the few widely circulated albums and their standout drum tracks.

amazighahwashandah.basis: Published LP/CD field recordings found: about a dozen tracks across five or six releases; the CREM-CNRS archive alone holds dozens of unpublished ahwash and ahidus items (e.g. multiple AHIDUS and AHWAS series from 1969-1979), the Lomax 1967 Morocco set has 15+ ahwash parts, and a local cassette/online market of named troupes (e.g. Khenifra bendir singers) adds an uncounted body. Core = the handful of anthologised tracks and the 1979 Ahwach LP.

cheo.basis: Chèo has roughly 200 traditional melodies (172 collected by Trần Vinh) and only about seven surviving classic plays, recorded mostly by state troupes, Vietnamese radio and domestic CD/VCD labels; each melody and famous play excerpt exists in several singers' versions, giving hundreds to a few thousand recordings, of which the classic-play excerpts and best-known melodies sung by the senior masters (a few dozen) would be called essential.

catru.basis: 56 named forms (thể cách) and a small revival scene (140 performers in 23 clubs by 2011, per Wikipedia); a handful of international label albums (UNESCO/Folkways, Inédit, Nimbus, Buda) of 7-10 tracks each plus Vietnamese CDs and broadcast/archive recordings. Core = the main forms (Bắc phản, Mưỡu, Hát nói, Tỳ bà hành, Thét nhạc, Gửi thư, Ba mươi sáu giọng, etc.) in a few master recordings.

quanho.basis: UNESCO counts 213 melody variants carrying 400+ lyrics; Nhân Dân (2009) reports 200+ melodies and 500+ collected songs. Many melodies have been recorded more than once by state troupes, village clubs and broadcasters, but few are on labelled international releases (one UNESCO/Folkways LP, a few CDs). Core = the welcome, invitation and farewell songs every club sings.

bihusongs.basis: A 2007 report gives about 100 Bihu cassettes a year plus 30-50 VCDs a season. At roughly 8-10 songs per album over about 40 years of cassette, VCD and online releases, that is some tens of thousands of songs. Add older HMV and radio recordings, and YouTube singles since 2010 that no source counts. The core figure is a guess at the classic Mahanta, Hazarika and Zubeen-era songs every Assamese listener knows.

pungmul.basis: One family of singers recorded 460 of a stated 4,000 orally transmitted folk songs for a single 8-CD set, and Arirang alone has over 100 regional versions; add decades of Korean LP/CD minyo anthologies (one compilation alone has 61 tracks) plus a smaller body of pungmul and samul nori albums (dozens of troupes since 1978). Recordings of minyo far outnumber percussion recordings. Core = the standard Arirang variants, the main Gyeonggi, Namdo and Seodo songs, and the classic SamulNori pieces.
